subsystems.name: Engineered skin cells
subsystems.role: the living light source: keratinocytes and fibroblasts in the dermis and basal layer that carry and express the inserted genes.
parts: basal-layer stem cells (needed for the glow to persist as skin renews)

subsystems.name: Light-producing gene cassette
subsystems.role: the DNA that the cells read to make a glowing protein.
parts: enzyme gene (firefly luciferase, a marine coelenterazine-based system such as aequorin, or the bacterial lux operon)

subsystems.name: Substrate supply
subsystems.role: luciferases need a chemical fuel; the glow is limited by how much is available where.
parts: or an engineered biosynthesis pathway that makes its own substrate

subsystems.name: Delivery and engraftment
subsystems.role: gets the cassette into enough long-lived skin cells.
parts: ex vivo: biopsy, edit, culture, graft back
or in vivo: lipid nanoparticles, viral vectors or microneedle injection

subsystems.name: Optical output
subsystems.role: how much light leaves the body, which depends on wavelength and skin pigments.
parts: luciferase emission colour (blue-green, ~470-560 nm; red-shifted variants reach further)

subsystems.name: Safety and control
subsystems.role: keeps the modification stable, switchable and non-harmful.

buildSteps.title: Choose the chemistry
buildSteps.detail: Decide between a self-contained bacterial lux operon, which makes its own fuel but is foreign to human cells, and firefly or coelenterazine systems, which glow brightly but need a substrate supplied from outside.

buildSteps.title: Design the cassette
buildSteps.detail: Assemble a codon-optimised gene under a promoter active in skin, with an inducible element so the glow can be switched on and off rather than running constantly.

buildSteps.title: Test in cultured skin cells
buildSteps.detail: Insert the cassette into human keratinocytes and fibroblasts in the lab, add substrate, and measure how much light survives through a layer of real skin tissue.

buildSteps.title: Graft into animal models
buildSteps.detail: Grow engineered human skin equivalents and graft them onto immunodeficient animals to see whether edited cells survive, renew and keep glowing.

buildSteps.title: Edit and graft human skin
buildSteps.detail: Take a small biopsy, edit the cells outside the body, expand them, and graft the sheet back — the approach already used to replace skin in severe burns and blistering diseases.

buildSteps.title: Improve brightness
buildSteps.detail: Use brighter and red-shifted enzyme variants, add substrate-recycling enzymes, and target cells nearer the surface so less light is absorbed.

buildSteps.title: Reach the stem cells
buildSteps.detail: Ensure the basal-layer stem cells are edited, not just the surface cells, or the glow fades within weeks as skin turns over.

buildSteps.title: Clear safety and regulation
buildSteps.detail: Screen for off-target edits, check the cells are not cancerous and not rejected, and obtain approval — currently no regulator permits gene editing purely for appearance.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Long-term follow-up for immune reactions, fading or unwanted growth, with a way to remove the modified patch if needed.

prerequisites.tech: Precise gene insertion in human somatic cells
prerequisites.why: CRISPR-based editing of human cells is routine in laboratories and now used in licensed therapies.
cultured skin sheets and gene-corrected grafts are established clinical practice for burns and severe skin-blistering disease.
substrate-making pathways have been moved whole into other organisms to create glowing plants, but never into human skin.

prerequisites.tech: Efficient editing of skin stem cells
prerequisites.why: without editing the basal stem cells, the glow disappears as the skin renews.
skin pigments absorb most visible light, so emitted light is very dim and mostly blue-green, which penetrates worst.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory and ethical framework for enhancement
prerequisites.why: somatic gene editing is approved only for serious disease, not for cosmetic traits.

pathway.milestone: bioluminescent cells, mice and plants in laboratories, plus a novelty glowing houseplant on sale
pathway.unlocks: proof that light-producing pathways work in living tissue.

pathway.milestone: engineered human skin equivalents glowing in the lab and on grafted animals
pathway.unlocks: evidence that edited skin survives, renews and stays dimly visible.

pathway.milestone: first human use, most plausibly as a medical marker to track a graft or a treated skin patch
pathway.unlocks: safety data on editing skin in people.

pathway.milestone: cosmetic clinics offering edited skin, if regulators ever permit non-medical editing
pathway.unlocks: a permanent, controllable glow — realistically decorative and very dim, not a display or a language.
